title: Abelard and Heloise
hookLine: a teacher who asked yes-and-no questions, and a brilliant abbess with her own theology
carry: by doubting we come to inquiry

cards: A boy is missing. His parents search the city, and when they finally find him, he's in the temple, among the teachers. Luke says he was "both hearing them, and asking them questions."
That boy is Jesus. Much later, a teacher in Paris named Peter Abelard points to this very scene to defend something risky: asking questions about the faith out loud.
And among the people he taught was a young woman with a mind of her own, named Heloise.

teach.h: SIC ET NON: YES AND NO.
teach.b: Abelard made a strange book called Sic et Non, Latin for yes and no. He gathered sayings from the church fathers on one question after another, and set them side by side where they seemed to disagree.
Yes, says one teacher. No, says another. He didn't settle the questions for his readers.

teach.h: WHY THE FATHERS SEEM TO CLASH.
teach.b: In the preface, he gives reasons the fathers might seem to clash: a word used in different senses, a saying wrongly credited, a copy made badly, a teacher who changed his mind. Then comes today's line.

teach.h: BY DOUBTING WE COME TO INQUIRY.
teach.b: By doubting, Abelard writes, we come to inquiry, and by inquiring we perceive the truth. And he points to Jesus himself: "Seek, and ye shall find." His own story was not peaceful.
His love affair with Heloise ended in scandal and a violent attack on him, and both of them entered religious life. Some of his teaching was condemned in his lifetime.
Heloise became an abbess, leading a community of nuns. Her letters to Abelard are fierce and honest.

teach.h: HELOISE: THE INTENTION OF THE HEART.
teach.b: She argues that what makes an act good or bad is the intention of the heart, not only the outward deed. She asks him to write a rule fit for women, not one borrowed from men.
And she sends him a list of hard questions about puzzling passages in the Bible, asking him to answer them for her nuns. Two people, both convinced that faith can bear honest questions.
Christians still disagree about how far doubt should go. But the boy in the temple asked.

how: Christians bring hard questions to Bible studies, classes, pastors and spiritual directors.

o: a teacher and an abbess who prized honest questions
two saints who wrote the rule for every convent
two monks who copied the church fathers' books

games.q: Abelard and Heloise — tap the pairs.

s: in Sic et Non, Abelard settles every question for his readers
he sets opposing sayings side by side and leaves readers to inquire.
Heloise argued that the intention of the heart matters, not only the outward deed
she says so in her letters to Abelard.
Abelard thought the fathers clashed because they were foolish
he gives other reasons: words in different senses, wrong credits, bad copies, changed minds.

games.q: you're Abelard. the church fathers seem to disagree with each other on a question. what do you do?
o: hide the disagreement so no one doubts.
pick the teacher you like and ignore the rest.
set the sayings side by side and ask why they differ.
games.why: he lined them up, yes and no, and argued that doubting leads to inquiry and inquiry to truth.

practice: Let one real question rise, about faith, about God, about something you were taught and never quite understood.
Say it plainly, inside, the way Heloise wrote hers down, and notice how it feels to hold a question without forcing it closed. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Abelard and Heloise. A teacher who set the fathers' yes and no side by side, and an abbess with her own sharp theology, both sure that honest questions lead toward truth.

orig.note: Latin: yes and no, the title of Abelard's book of seemingly opposing sayings.

carryVoice: Your line: by doubting we come to inquiry. And by inquiring, Abelard says, we perceive the truth. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: both hearing them, and asking them questions.
